sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 79 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: Help us for the glory of Your name
study.intro: Asaph's community laments Jerusalem in ruins and its people slain, then asks God to forgive, rescue and act for His own name's sake, ending with a promise of lasting praise.
study.context: Psalm 79 is headed 'A Psalm of Asaph.' It mourns the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, most naturally read alongside the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC described in 2 Kings 25 and Lamentations. Like Psalm 74 it is a community lament. It moves from describing the disaster (verses 1–4), to asking 'How long?' (verse 5), to petitions for forgiveness and rescue (verses 6–12), and closes with a vow of thanks (verse 13). Jeremiah 10:25 closely echoes verses 6–7.
study.peopleNote: The heading names Asaph, the Levite worship leader appointed by David; the app has no Asaph profile yet, so no person card is linked. Verse 7 names Jacob as a name for the whole nation, pointing back to the patriarch Jacob, who has a profile in the app. Planned paintings would show ruins, mourners and sheep in pasture, never graphic violence; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: The city in rubble
verses.heading: When the holy place falls
verses.meaning: The heading names Asaph. Then the lament begins: 'The nations, O God, have invaded Your inheritance; they have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble.' The people bring the disaster straight to God and describe it as His loss: His inheritance, His temple. Honest lament does not soften the facts. It tells God exactly what has happened and trusts Him to care, because what belongs to His people ultimately belongs to Him.
verses.context: 2 Kings 25:8-10 records Babylon burning the temple and breaking down Jerusalem's walls. Lamentations 1:10 grieves that the nations entered the sanctuary. Psalm 74:3 makes a similar plea about the ruins.
explore: Inheritance
The land and people God claimed as His own special possession, given to Israel as a lasting gift.
Defiled
Made ritually unclean or profaned, treating what is holy as common and polluting God's dwelling place.
verses.reflect: What loss in your life or community do you need to describe honestly to God today?
verses.alt: Broken stone walls and toppled pillars of an ancient city under a gray sky.

verses.title: No honor for the fallen
verses.heading: Grief over the unburied
verses.meaning: Verse 2 grieves: 'They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of Your saints to the beasts of the earth.' In the ancient world an unburied body was the deepest dishonor. The psalm calls the dead God's servants and saints, insisting they still belong to Him. Scripture does not look away from the horror of war, and it gives grieving people words to bring that horror before God.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 28:26 warns of bodies left for birds as a covenant curse. Jeremiah 7:33 repeats the warning before Jerusalem's fall. Psalm 116:15 says the death of His saints is precious in the LORD's sight.
explore: Saints
People set apart as belonging to God, His faithful ones, not a special class but His covenant people.
Unburied dead
A sign of total defeat and dishonor in ancient Israel, where proper burial showed love and respect.
verses.reflect: How does it comfort you that God calls His suffering people 'His saints' even in defeat?
verses.alt: Mourners in head cloths stand quietly beside a ruined city gate at dusk.

verses.title: Blood like water
verses.heading: No one left to bury
verses.meaning: Verse 3 continues: 'They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury the dead.' The image is of life spilled carelessly and in great quantity. Worse still, so many have died or fled that no one remains to perform the last act of love. The psalm lets grief be as large as the loss. God invites us to name the full weight of sorrow instead of hurrying past it.
verses.context: Lamentations 2:21 describes the young and old lying in the streets. Jeremiah 14:16 speaks of no one to bury them. Matthew 5:4 promises that those who mourn will be comforted.
explore: Lament
A prayer of sorrow and complaint brought to God, a form of faith that refuses to stop talking to Him.
Poured out like water
A picture of something spent freely and without value placed on it, here describing lives cruelly taken.
verses.reflect: Is there a grief you have hurried past that you need to bring to God more fully?
verses.alt: An empty hillside path outside city walls, with scattered stones and withered grass.

verses.title: Mocked by the neighbors
verses.heading: Living under scorn
verses.meaning: Verse 4 adds social shame: 'We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a scorn and derision to those around us.' Beyond physical loss, the people endure ridicule from surrounding nations who watch their downfall with contempt. Shame can wound as deeply as violence. The psalmist does not hide that pain either. Bringing humiliation to God is part of healing, because He sees what others mock.
verses.context: Obadiah 1:12 rebukes Edom for gloating over Judah's disaster. Psalm 44:13 uses nearly the same words. Lamentations 2:15 describes passersby who clap and hiss at Jerusalem.
explore: Reproach
Public disgrace or contempt heaped on someone, making them an object of insult among others.
Derision
Mocking laughter and scorn that treats a person or people as foolish and worthless.
verses.reflect: When have you felt mocked or shamed, and what would it mean to let God see that wound?
verses.alt: Distant figures on a ridge look down toward a ruined city in the valley below.

verses.title: How long, O LORD?
verses.heading: The cry of a long sorrow
verses.meaning: Verse 5 asks: 'How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever? Will Your jealousy burn like fire?' The people recognize that their disaster is connected to God's judgment on their unfaithfulness. His jealousy is His fierce covenant love that will not share His people with idols. Yet they ask whether it will last forever. The question itself is hopeful: it assumes God's anger has limits and His mercy can return.
verses.context: Exodus 34:14 says the LORD's name is Jealous. Psalm 89:46 asks the same 'How long?' question. Isaiah 54:8 promises that God's anger lasts a moment but His compassion is everlasting.
explore: Jealousy of God
God's protective, exclusive love for His people that burns against anything that steals their devotion.
How long
A common lament cry that admits pain while still expecting God to act at the right time.
verses.reflect: What 'How long?' question are you carrying, and can you bring it to God as an act of trust?
verses.alt: A lone figure sits on a stone step, head bowed, as smoke drifts over distant hills.

verses.title: Turn Your wrath outward
verses.heading: Nations that refuse God
verses.meaning: Verse 6 prays: 'Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, on the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name.' The request contrasts Israel, who still calls on God, with nations who ignore Him and destroy His people. It is a plea for justice, not personal revenge. The psalmist leaves judgment in God's hands. Later Scripture shows God's heart to bring even those nations to call on His name.
verses.context: Jeremiah 10:25 repeats this verse almost word for word. Romans 12:19 tells believers to leave vengeance to God. Zephaniah 3:9 foresees nations calling on the name of the LORD.
explore: Wrath
God's settled, just opposition to evil, not a temper but a holy response to sin and cruelty.
Call on His name
To pray to God and worship Him, depending on Him by name as one's own Lord.
verses.reflect: How can you bring your desire for justice to God without letting it turn into personal revenge?
verses.alt: Dark storm clouds gather over a range of distant mountains.

verses.title: They devoured Jacob
verses.heading: A homeland laid waste
verses.meaning: Verse 7 explains the plea: 'for they have devoured Jacob and devastated his homeland.' The nation is called by the name of its ancestor Jacob, reminding God of His promises to the patriarch. The enemies have swallowed the people like a beast consuming prey and turned their pastures to waste. The psalmist appeals to God's long history with this family as the reason He should act now.
verses.context: Genesis 28:13-14 records God's promise of land and offspring to Jacob. Jeremiah 10:25 completes this same lament. Isaiah 41:14 calls the people 'O worm Jacob' and promises help.
explore: Jacob
The patriarch renamed Israel, whose name became a poetic title for the whole nation descended from him.
Homeland
The land of promise, here meaning the pastures and dwelling places where God's people lived.
verses.reflect: Which of God's past promises to His people can you lean on when your own life feels devastated?
verses.alt: Abandoned terraced fields and a broken stone sheepfold on a hillside.

verses.title: Do not hold past sins
verses.heading: Mercy, and quickly
verses.meaning: Verse 8 turns to confession: 'Do not hold past sins against us; let Your compassion come quickly, for we are brought low.' The people do not claim innocence. They ask God not to keep counting the sins of earlier generations or their own former wrongs. Their urgency is plain: they are brought very low and need mercy now. God's compassion is the only hope for people who know they deserve less.
verses.context: Lamentations 5:7 says, 'Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their iniquities.' Psalm 103:10 says God does not deal with us according to our sins. Micah 7:19 promises He will cast our sins into the depths of the sea.
explore: Past sins
The wrongs of earlier generations or one's own former failures that seem to bring ongoing consequences.
Compassion
God's tender, motherly mercy that moves Him to care for the suffering and the guilty.
verses.reflect: What past failure do you need to hand to God, trusting Him not to hold it against you?
verses.alt: A humble person kneels on a dusty path with open hands as morning light breaks.

verses.title: For the sake of Your name
verses.heading: Atonement and rescue
verses.meaning: Verse 9 prays: 'Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of Your name; deliver us and atone for our sins, for the sake of Your name.' The people appeal not to their own merit but to God's reputation. They ask for rescue from enemies and for atonement, the covering of their sin. Both come from God alone. The strongest prayers rest on who God is rather than on who we are.
verses.context: Leviticus 16:30 describes the Day of Atonement cleansing the people. Ezekiel 36:22 says God acts for the sake of His holy name. 1 John 2:2 says Jesus is the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
explore: Atone
To cover or remove sin so that a guilty person can be reconciled to God, ultimately accomplished through Christ.
For His name's sake
Acting to display and honor God's own character and reputation rather than because people deserve it.
verses.reflect: How does praying 'for the sake of Your name' change the way you ask God for help?
verses.alt: A clay altar with rising smoke stands on a quiet hilltop at dawn.

verses.title: Where is their God?
verses.heading: God's honor among the nations
verses.meaning: Verse 10 asks: 'Why should the nations ask, “Where is their God?” Before our eyes, make known among the nations Your vengeance for the bloodshed of Your servants.' The enemies' taunt questions God's existence and power. The psalmist wants God to answer it publicly by bringing justice for innocent blood. God's justice is not only for His people's relief; it shows the world that He is real and righteous.
verses.context: Joel 2:17 uses the same taunt in a call to prayer. Psalm 115:2 answers it: 'Our God is in heaven.' Revelation 6:10 records martyrs asking how long until their blood is avenged.
explore: Vengeance of God
God's just repayment of evil, a right He keeps for Himself and exercises with perfect fairness.
Bloodshed
The killing of innocent people, which Scripture says cries out to God from the ground.
verses.reflect: When others question where God is in your hardship, how might you answer them honestly?
verses.alt: Travelers on a road point toward a ruined city while others look up at the sky.

verses.title: Groans of the captives
verses.heading: Strength to save the condemned
verses.meaning: Verse 11 prays: 'May the groans of the captives reach You; by the strength of Your arm preserve those condemned to death.' The prayer remembers prisoners taken away and people awaiting execution. Their sighs may be wordless, yet the psalmist asks God to hear them. God's arm is a picture of His power to rescue. No prisoner is beyond His reach, and no groan is too faint for Him to notice.
verses.context: Exodus 6:6 promises redemption 'with an outstretched arm.' Psalm 102:20 says the LORD looks down to hear the groaning of prisoners. Romans 8:26 says the Spirit intercedes with groans too deep for words.
explore: Captives
People taken prisoner and carried away by conquerors, often into exile in a foreign land.
Strength of Your arm
A biblical picture of God's mighty power at work to save and protect His people.
verses.reflect: Who do you know who feels trapped or condemned, and how can you pray for them today?
verses.alt: A line of captives in rope bonds walks along a desert road under a wide sky.

verses.title: Sevenfold into their laps
verses.heading: Justice for insults against God
verses.meaning: Verse 12 asks: 'Pay back into the laps of our neighbors sevenfold the reproach they hurled at You, O Lord.' The fold of a robe was used to carry grain, so the image is of a full measure poured back on those who mocked. Notice the insult was hurled at God. The psalmist is jealous for God's honor. He asks God to settle the account fully, rather than taking revenge himself.
verses.context: Luke 6:38 uses the same picture of a measure poured into your lap. Genesis 4:15 speaks of sevenfold vengeance. Proverbs 24:29 warns against saying, 'I will repay him.'
explore: Sevenfold
A full and complete measure, seven being the biblical number of completeness.
Lap
The fold of a long robe, held out to carry grain or goods, picturing a generous or full repayment.
verses.reflect: Are you trying to defend God's honor yourself, or trusting Him to settle what is His to settle?
verses.alt: A harvester holds out the fold of a robe as grain is poured into it.

verses.title: Sheep of Your pasture
verses.heading: Praise from generation to generation
verses.meaning: Verse 13 ends in hope: 'Then we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever; from generation to generation we will declare Your praise.' After all the ruin, the people still call themselves God's flock. They promise lasting thanks and to pass praise on to their children. Lament ends in a vow of worship, because the Shepherd has not abandoned His sheep.
verses.context: Psalm 100:3 says, 'We are His people, the sheep of His pasture.' Psalm 78:4 commits to telling the next generation. John 10:11 presents Jesus as the good shepherd who lays down His life.
explore: Sheep of His pasture
God's people pictured as a flock He owns, feeds and guards as their shepherd.
Generation to generation
Passing faith and praise from parents to children so that God's works are never forgotten.
verses.reflect: What story of God's faithfulness could you pass on to someone younger this week?
verses.alt: A flock of sheep grazes on a green hillside as a shepherd watches at sunrise.
